title: Saying No: Negation
description: Two kinds of 'no': ما…ش wrapped around a verb, مش in front of everything else. Never, nobody, not yet and nothing at all — and the art of refusing a plate of food three times without offending anyone.
approach: GPA Phase 2 — every negative is heard as the reply to a positive first (تشتي شاهي؟ — ما اشتيش), so the shape is learned as a response before it is analysed.
unlock_condition: ≥10/14 on the make-it-negative drill and a recorded polite refusal

grammar.title: Two kinds of no: ما…ش for verbs, مش for everything else
grammar.explanation: A verb is negated by putting ما before it and hanging -ش on the end: ما أعرفش, 'I don't know'; ما سرتش, 'I didn't go'. The same wrapper goes round عندي and فيه: ما عنديش، ما فيش. Anything that is not a verb — a noun, an adjective, a place — takes مش in front and nothing on the end: هو مش مهندس, الجو مش بارد. Sanaa also says ماش for the same thing, and you will hear مو from Gulf-facing speakers. Never ليس.

examples.english: I didn't go to the market yesterday
He's not an engineer, he's a teacher

grammar.title: Don't do it: just لا
grammar.explanation: Telling someone not to do something needs only لا and the 'you' form of the verb — no ما, no -ش: لا تجي بكرة, 'don't come tomorrow'. To a woman the verb ends in -i, to a group in -u. Said with a smile it is advice; said sharp it is an order.

culture.title: The first no is not a no
culture.note: When food or a second helping is offered, the guest refuses; the host insists; the guest refuses again; the host insists harder. Only the third refusal counts, and a host who gives up after one thinks you are unhappy. So your first لا should be soft — والله شبعت, 'honestly I'm full' — and if you really mean it, add the blessing: الله يعافيكم. To accept, just stop refusing. Never say مستحيل about food; that word is for prices and plans.

phrases.english: I don't want more, bless you

culture.title: Saying no without saying no
culture.note: A direct refusal of a request or invitation makes someone lose face, so real refusals are wrapped: 'God willing', 'we'll see', 'maybe later', or a reason that is nobody's fault. إن شاء الله with no time attached is a gentle no; an apology with معليش softens a definite one. Learn to hear these as well as say them.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The 'not' that goes in front of anything that is not a verb. Sanaa also says ماش (maash); مو is Gulf-flavoured but heard. Never ليس — a learner who says it sounds like a newsreader.
vocabulary.image_scene: A plate crossed out in red beside an identical plate untouched.
vocabulary.video_hint: Any 'I'm not…', 'it's not…' in dialogue; usually followed by an adjective.

vocabulary.teaching_note: A wrapper, not a word: ما goes before the verb and -ش glues to its end. The -ش is optional in careful speech but nearly everyone uses it. Before ولا ('nor / at all') the -ش is dropped: ما أكلت ولا حاجة.
vocabulary.image_scene: A person shaking their head while pushing away a glass of tea.

example.english: I don't drink coffee at night

vocabulary.video_hint: Negated verbs in speech; the -sh is audible at the end of the verb.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Goes with a negated verb to mean never, or stands alone as 'not at all!' in reply to thanks or apology. Keeps its -an ending. عمري ما, 'in my life I haven't', is the other way to say never.
vocabulary.image_scene: A calendar with every day crossed out in red.
vocabulary.video_hint: Emphatic denials; 'never!' as a standalone reply.

vocabulary.teaching_note: ما أحد squeezed into one word with a doubled ح — very Sanaa. It stands as the subject with no further negation: محّد يعرفني هنا. Hold the double ḥ or it becomes 'mahad'.
vocabulary.image_scene: An empty mafraj with cushions and no one in it.
vocabulary.video_hint: An empty room or unanswered door: 'there's nobody'.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Literally 'and not a thing'. Yemenis use حاجة for 'thing' alongside شي, so ولا شي is just as common. Note the verb before it loses its -ش: ما أكلت ولا حاجة.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two empty open hands held out over an empty table.

example.english: I haven't eaten a thing today

vocabulary.video_hint: 'I didn't do anything', 'there's nothing' in skits.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Sanaa's 'still' is عاد, and it takes a pronoun: عادني ('I'm still'), عادك, عاده. With a negative verb after it, it means 'not yet': عادني ما تغدّيت. لسه ما is the imported alternative.
vocabulary.image_scene: A clock face and an empty lunch plate, someone checking their watch.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The most frequent word in Yemeni speech. After a noun it means 'only' (شاهي بس); at the start of a clause it means 'but'; alone, with a raised hand, it means 'enough!'. One word, three jobs.
vocabulary.image_scene: A single glass of tea on an otherwise empty tray.
vocabulary.video_hint: Everywhere; listen for it closing an order or a sentence.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The clear 'but' for contrasting two things. بس does the same job more casually; لكن is a touch more deliberate. Long aa in the first syllable.
vocabulary.image_scene: A beautiful house with a large price tag hanging on the door.

example.english: The house is nice but expensive

vocabulary.video_hint: Contrasts in reviews and complaints: 'nice, but…'.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Closes a subject: the food, the argument, the bargaining. Also 'it's settled' or 'finished'. Emphatic ص at the end; the aa is long.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand held palm-out over a plate, the eater leaning back.
vocabulary.video_hint: Ending a meal, a deal or a quarrel with one word.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The flat 'no way' — for a price, a plan, a claim. Too strong for food or a person's invitation. ما يمكن, 'can't be', is the milder cousin.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man throwing both hands up in front of a price board.
vocabulary.video_hint: Outraged reactions in comedy; bargaining breakdowns.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The verb you know, اشتي, wrapped in ما…ش. Add the thing (ما اشتيش سكر) or a verb (ما اشتيش أسير). Softer with شكراً after it.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand gently covering the top of a tea glass as sugar is offered.

example.english: I don't want sugar, thank you

vocabulary.video_hint: Refusals at the table or in a shop: 'I don't want…'.

vocabulary.english: it doesn't matter / no big deal
vocabulary.teaching_note: Literally 'normal'. The reply that dissolves a problem: no bread? عادي. Late? عادي. ما عليك, 'don't worry about it', and معليش, 'never mind', are the other two in the set.
vocabulary.image_scene: A shrug with a relaxed smile, a spilled tea glass on the table.
vocabulary.video_hint: The shrugging reply to a small mishap.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Three jobs: 'or' in a question (شاهي ولا قهوة؟), 'nor' after a negative, and 'not even one' before a noun (ولا واحد). The verb before it drops its -ش.
vocabulary.image_scene: A tray with tea and coffee, both pushed away, a glass of water pulled close.

example.arabic: لا شاهي ولا قهوة، مي بس
example.transliteration: laa shaahi wala gahwa, mi bass
example.english: Neither tea nor coffee, just water

vocabulary.teaching_note: Enough of an amount — sugar, rice, talk. خلاص closes the subject; كفاية measures it. Often paired: بس كفاية.
vocabulary.image_scene: A spoon held up to stop more sugar going into a glass.
vocabulary.video_hint: Someone signalling 'enough' while food or drink is being served.

vocabulary.english: in the first place / at all
vocabulary.teaching_note: Sharpens a negative: 'he didn't even come'. Keeps its -an ending. Also 'anyway' at the start of a sentence.
vocabulary.image_scene: An empty chair at a dinner table with an untouched plate.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The highland twin of ما فيش, from به 'there is'. Hearing مابش tells you the speaker is from Sanaa or the north. Write ما فيش as two words when you use that one.
vocabulary.image_scene: An empty water jug tipped over a glass, nothing coming out.

example.english: There's no water in the house

vocabulary.video_hint: Sanaa speakers saying 'there's no…' — power, water, bread.

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.english: No really, I'm full. That's it.

dialogue.speaker: Hussein
dialogue.english: Impossible! You haven't eaten a thing.

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.arabic: أكلت كثير، لكن ما اشتيش زيادة.
dialogue.transliteration: akalt kathiir, laakin maa ashtiish ziyaada.
dialogue.english: I ate a lot, but I don't want any more.

dialogue.speaker: Hussein
dialogue.arabic: بدون سكر؟ محّد يشرب شاهي بدون سكر هنا!
dialogue.transliteration: biduun sukkar? maḥḥad yishrab shaahi biduun sukkar hina!
dialogue.english: Without sugar? Nobody drinks tea without sugar here!

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.english: No big deal — I'm not from here.

sound_spotlight.explanation: The negative -sh is a whispered consonant tacked straight on, not a new syllable. sirt-sh, not sirt-ish.
Two ḥ sounds held long in the middle; the doubling is what separates 'nobody' from a name.
Same word, short or long vowel. Sanaa speakers use both; maash is a touch more emphatic.

lesson_sequence.detail: Each positive sentence from earlier lessons plays with its negative reply: تشتي شاهي؟ — ما اشتيش. Pictures show the refusal.
Drag words into two bins — verb or not-a-verb — and hear the app negate each with ما…ش or مش.
Hear a sentence, say the negative; the app checks for ما, -ش or مش.
Cards for أبداً، محّد، ولا حاجة، عاد ما with one example each; listen-and-tap.
Role-play with Hussein: refuse the plate three times with escalating phrases, then accept tea.
Counter rolls up; nudge to use عادي once tomorrow.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Next time you are offered food, refuse once with والله شبعت — then watch the host insist, and accept.
real_world_prompts.context: Shown on completion. Activates the refusal ritual and شبعت.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Say what you don't do: ما أشربش قهوة، ما أخزّنش. Three sentences out loud.
real_world_prompts.context: Production prompt for the ما…ش wrapper.

real_world_prompts.prompt: When something small goes wrong today, say عادي and mean it.
real_world_prompts.context: Habit prompt for the most useful reaction word in the lesson.

video_needs.scene: Someone declining, arguing or refusing on camera — a guest waving away food, a buyer saying 'no way', a character insisting 'I didn't do anything'.
